meta.title: Report of the work undertaken by the Cookie Banner Taskforce

section.title: Type A practice – “No reject button on the first layer”
section.paragraph: As a preliminary remark, the task force members recalled that by default, no cookies which require consent can be set without a consent and that consent must be expressed by a positive action on the part of the user.

When authorities were asked whether they would consider that a banner which does not provide for accept and refuse/reject/not consent options on any layer with a consent button is an infringement of the ePrivacy Directive, a vast majority of authorities considered that the absence of refuse/reject/not consent options on any layer with a consent button of the cookie consent banner is not in line with the requirements for a valid consent and thus constitutes an infringement. Few authorities considered that they cannot retain an infringement in this case as article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive does not explicitly mentioned a “reject option” to the deposit of cookies.

section.title: Type B practice – “Pre-ticked boxes”
section.paragraph: The taskforce members confirmed that pre-ticked boxes to opt-in do not lead to valid consent as referred to either in the GDPR (see in particular recital 32 “Silence, pre-ticked boxes or inactivity should not therefore constitute consent.”) or in Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive.

section.title: Type C practice – Deceptive “Link Design”
section.paragraph: The members agreed that for the consent to be valid, the user should be able to understand what they consent to and how to do so. In order for a valid consent to be freely given, the taskforce members agreed that in any case a website owner must not design cookie banners in a way that gives users the impression that they have to give a consent to access the website content, nor that clearly pushes the user to give consent (one way could be on the contrary to allow the continuation of the navigation without cookies from the first level in particular for example).

section.title: Type D & E practices: “Deceptive button colours” & “deceptive button contrast”
section.paragraph:
Based on concrete examples, the taskforce members took the view that at least this practice could be manifestly misleading for users:
an alternative action is offered (other than granting consent) in the form of a button where the contrast between the text and the button background is so minimal that the text is unreadable to virtually any user.

section.title: Type H practice: “Legitimate interest claimed, list of purposes”
section.paragraph: In this regard, the taskforce members took the view that non-compliance found concerning Art. 5 (3) in the ePrivacy directive (in particular when no valid consent is obtained where required), means that the subsequent processing cannot be compliant with the GDPR. Also, the TF members confirmed that the legal basis for the placement/reading of cookies pursuant to Article 5 (3) cannot be the legitimate interests of the controller.

section.title: Type K practice: “No withdraw icon”
section.paragraph: Website owners should put in place easily accessible solutions allowing users to withdraw their consent at any time, such as an icon (small hovering and permanently visible icon) or a link placed on a visible and standardized place.

In addition to the requirements for the collection of consent to be valid in accordance with the GDPR and under Article 5(3) ePrivacy Directive, three additional cumulative conditions are mandatory (i) the possibility to withdraw consent, (ii) the ability to withdraw consent at any time, (iii) withdrawal of consent must be as easy as to give consent.
